## At the Court

Last week, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on its emergency docket to clear the way for the implementation of President Donald Trump’s executive order on mail-in voting. Twelve states – led by Alabama – later echoed this request in their own application. On Monday, the group of 23 states and the District of Columbia challenging the order urged the court to deny these requests. The matter is now fully briefed, and the court’s ruling could come at any time. results.title: Potential refunds: US Supreme Court overturns IEEPA tariffs | Global law firm | Norton Rose Fulbright
results.content: While the CIT is empowered to order particular administrative remedies for issuing refunds to importers, it is more likely to, as it has done in the past, leave such administrative procedures to US Customs to develop and implement. US Customs typically implements such procedures through formal guidance to importers either published in the Federal Register or through its Cargo Systems Messaging Service (CSMS). Such guidance usually entails directing importers to seek refunds by filing [...] Accordingly, following the Supreme Court’s decision today, and per US Customs regulations, the US government no longer has any authority to continue collecting the tariffs and must, at least insofar as the importer has properly preserved its rights, refund any such tariff amounts already collected. Where entries have already liquidated, Customs may also be required to pay interest to importers in addition to the amount of invalid tariffs paid. [...] In a landmark 6 – 3 decision, the US Supreme Court held today that the President lacks authority to impose any tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). 24-1287 Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (02/20/2026). The decision has sweeping implications for US importers and purchasers of US imported products as it effectively rules that all of the tariffs imposed under IEEPA are, and have been since inception, invalid.

results.title: One Small Step for Importers: Federal Circuit Clears the Way for IEEPA Tariff Refund Litigation to Resume | Buchalter
results.content: Refund claimants secured an important procedural victory on March 2, 2026, when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit denied the government a stay and ordered V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. Trump, Case No. 25-1812, remanded back to the U.S. Court of International Trade (CIT). While procedural in nature, the decision marks another step forward for importers seeking refunds of tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). [...] With the mandate issued, jurisdiction returns to the CIT where more than 2,000 similar tariff lawsuits have already been filed. Those cases were paused pending the Supreme Court’s decision. CIT is now expected to move forward. Key issues likely to be addressed include the mechanics and timing of refunds, treatment of liquidated versus unliquidated entries, administrative implementation by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and potential offsets, such as credits in lieu of refunds, or [...] After the Supreme Court ruled, the Justice Department asked the Federal Circuit to delay issuing its mandate to return the case to CIT. Specifically, the government requested that the court wait for the Supreme Court to formally finalize its judgment—a process that typically takes about 32 days—and then impose an additional 90-day stay before remanding the case. The government argued that the delay would allow Congress an opportunity to formulate a legislative solution for refunds.
